sections.h2: How unpaid Ohio property tax becomes a lien
sections.html:
The lien exists from the first day of each tax year. R.C. 323.11 says the state's lien for real property tax attaches on January 1 and lasts until the tax, penalties, interest and charges are paid. Your bill arrives later, but the claim on the parcel is already there.

That is why an unpaid balance cannot simply be left behind at a closing. If only part of a tract changes hands, the same section lets the tax be apportioned, and the lien then reaches each part only up to the amount allocated to it.

The county treasurer, working through the prosecuting attorney, files the foreclosure case. The owner gets several chances to pay before the property is sold.

sections.h2: When an Ohio county starts tax foreclosure
sections.html:
The treasurer may sue once taxes have gone unpaid for sixty days after the delinquent land duplicate is delivered to the treasurer. R.C. 323.25 lets the treasurer enforce the lien by civil action, the way a mortgage is foreclosed, in common pleas court, in a municipal court with jurisdiction, or before the county Board of Revision where that board has authority.

A second route appears in R.C. 5721.18. The prosecuting attorney files in the treasurer's name after the auditor delivers the delinquent land certificate or master list. An in rem action, one against the parcel itself, may be filed once the second year has ended from the date the delinquency was first certified.

The treasurer is barred from enforcing the lien in any of these situations:

  • The parcel has a pending application for exemption and is not on the delinquent land duplicate.
  • A valid delinquent tax contract is in force and has not been voided.
  • A tax certificate on the parcel has been sold, as to the taxes it covers.

Pay the delinquency or arrange a plan. R.C. 323.31 entitles an owner who lives in the home, or a land contract buyer who occupies it, to at least one written delinquent tax contract with the treasurer, provided no tax lien certificate or foreclosure judgment is outstanding. Residential contracts run up to five years, and at least two years if the owner asks. Any later contract is up to the treasurer.

You may sign the contract any time before the adjudication of foreclosure. It breaks if an installment is missed or the current taxes go unpaid, and the prosecuting attorney then files the foreclosure. If a tax certificate was sold, the owner uses a redemption payment plan under section 5721.38 instead.

The right to redeem stays open for a while after suit is filed. R.C. 5721.25 lets anyone entitled to redeem pay the taxes, assessments, penalties, interest, charges and costs to the treasurer before foreclosure begins. After filing, redemption remains possible until the entry confirming the sale, or until the alternative redemption period ends, but the owner must also show the property meets zoning, land use, building, health and safety codes. A delinquent tax contract can even be signed after filing, for up to five years, though the case keeps moving and the contract can end if the property falls out of code compliance.

sections.h2: Alternative redemption period and abandoned land
sections.html:
This is a short window after judgment. R.C. 323.65 defines it as twenty-eight days after the adjudication of foreclosure is journalized, ending on and including the twenty-eighth day. When it runs out, the owner's right and equity of redemption end with no further order. A county treasurer decides whether to invoke it under section 323.78.

If it is invoked and a city, township, county, school district, community development organization or land reutilization corporation has asked for the parcel, the court or board orders it deeded to that body without appraisal or sale, free of the taxes and other liens. If nobody asked, the parcel is sold in the usual way, and if no one bids it is forfeited to the state.

The expedited process for abandoned land turns on the word unoccupied. A parcel counts as unoccupied when no taxable building is lived in, no trade or business operates there, or the parcel is uninhabited with no sign of changed tenants or improvements. A presumption arises when the parcel is not agricultural and at least two of these are true at certification:

  • An exterior inspection by the county, municipality or township finds no person, trade or business present.
  • No utility connections serve it, or none are being billed.
  • It is boarded up or sealed after being found open, vacant or vandalized.
  • It is insecure, vacant or vandalized on visible inspection.

sections.h2: Stages of a county tax foreclosure
sections.html:
Ohio delinquent land tax enforcement, stage by stage
StageTiming or limit
Lien attachesJanuary 1 of each tax year
Suit by the treasurerAfter 60 days from delivery of the delinquent duplicate
Answer in an in rem actionWithin 28 days after service is complete
Payment planUp to 5 years for an owner-occupied home
Alternative redemption28 days after judgment is journalized
Second sale if no bidNot less than 2 or more than 6 weeks later

In an in rem case the answer deadline is the one to watch. Section 5721.18 allows a default judgment on any parcel without an answer, and it binds everyone with an interest, including people out of state.

Under R.C. 5721.19, the court may order a parcel sold without appraisal for no less than the lesser of two figures: the auditor's fair market value plus costs, or the total found due plus costs. If no bid reaches that figure, the sale is adjourned to a second date. If a sale brings in less than what is owed, the court may enter a deficiency judgment against the owner of record. A sale in an in rem case under division (B) gives the buyer title free of most liens, apart from a properly filed federal tax lien and earlier easements and covenants.

sections.h2: Selling the house or collecting leftover money
sections.html:
A sale does not end a case already filed. R.C. 5721.18(D) provides that a conveyance after the complaint is filed and before the foreclosure judgment does not cancel the county's right to proceed. Ask the treasurer and the prosecuting attorney for a payoff figure that includes the costs of the case, have it paid from the proceeds at closing, and get written confirmation that the case is resolved.

A sale of land for delinquent taxes carries no auditor's conveyance fee under R.C. 319.54, which lists transfers on sale for delinquent taxes among its exemptions.

When a foreclosure sale brings in more than the judgment, R.C. 5721.20 sends the excess to the clerk of court within forty-five days after confirmation, and the clerk notifies the owner. Money unclaimed within ninety days of the final notice goes to the county treasury, where the treasurer holds it for three years. After that it is forfeited to the delinquent tax and assessment collection fund, or to a land reutilization fund where the county has one.

faqs.q: How long can I be behind on Ohio property tax before foreclosure?
faqs.a: The treasurer may sue sixty days after the delinquent land duplicate is delivered. A prosecuting attorney in rem action can follow after the second year from first certification. The treasurer can tell you where your parcel stands.

faqs.q: Can I set up a payment plan for delinquent Ohio taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. An owner who lives in the home is entitled to at least one delinquent tax contract, running up to five years, or two if requested. No tax lien certificate or foreclosure judgment can be outstanding when the first contract is signed.

faqs.q: Can I still pay after the county files a tax foreclosure?
faqs.a: Yes. You can redeem by paying everything due plus costs before the entry confirming the sale, or before the alternative redemption period of twenty-eight days after judgment ends. The property must also meet local building and zoning codes.

faqs.q: What does the alternative redemption period mean?
faqs.a: It is the twenty-eight days after the court or Board of Revision journalizes the foreclosure judgment. Once it ends, the owner's right of redemption is gone with no further order. Only counties whose treasurer invokes it use it.

faqs.q: Do I get money back if my house sells for more than the taxes owed?
faqs.a: Yes. Excess proceeds go to the clerk, who notifies the owner. If it goes unclaimed for ninety days after the final notice, the county treasurer holds it, and the owner may demand it within three years.
